name: PT Samindo Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: Samindo Resources is priced as if the contract has already gone
frontmatter.summary: A coal-mining contractor, filed as one this time, with net cash close to its whole market value, a contracted book to the end of the decade and a nine-month profit up by half. We value the contract, the renewal and the cash separately, carry a contract-loss case at a material probability, and still start at Buy.
thesis: The market pays almost nothing for the operating business: cash and time deposits of US$60.9m and US$40.8m at September 2026 exceed the market capitalisation, and the shares trade on 1.2x trailing EBITDA with a trailing yield of 7.3% [S0, S3, F32, F33].

The earnings turn is in the filings, not in our forecast: nine-month revenue of US$133.1m, gross profit of US$34.5m and net profit to owners of US$17.4m, on overburden volume of 28.3 Mbcm [S3, S5, F31].
We value the contracted book with no terminal value at Rp1,288, a renewed book at Rp2,577, and the peer multiple at Rp3,546; the weights are an explicit renewal probability, not a smoothing [S2, S0].

The client is the company: Kideco paid US$133.8m of the US$164.0m revenue in FY2025 and the overburden contract expires at the end of 2029, so the contract-loss case carries a probability of 20.0% and a value of Rp1,455 [S2, F23, F1].
The assets the cash bought are in the bridge at cost: land of US$13.7m and a related-party loan of US$4.2m, both of which the previous file left out [S3, F35, F46].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Samindo Resources at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp1,757 and a total return of 105.5% against a share price of Rp900 [S0]. The target carries a 20.0% illiquidity discount, and it is built from a DCF of the contracted book to the end of the overburden contract, a FCFF DCF that pays for a renewal, and a contractor peer multiple, blended at weights that state a renewal probability and then rolled forward at the cost of equity [S0, S2].

This revision changes the classification, and the classification is the argument. Samindo owns no mine, sells no coal and books no royalty; it removes overburden, gets coal and hauls coal for a concession holder, and its own annual report gives the sub-industry as oil, gas and coal equipment and services [S2, p.40]. The earlier draft carried a coal producer label, which imported a producer peer multiple and a producer beta of 1.00 into a single-client service contract. The file now runs on the contractor card: the corporate template, a cost of capital built at an industry beta of 1.00 with a premium for concentration, and a peer set of listed Indonesian contractors with no producer among them [S0, S2].

What the market prices is not our view of coal. At Rp900 the equity is worth about what the group holds in cash and time deposits, which were US$60.9m and US$40.8m respectively at the end of September 2026 [S0, S3, F32, F33]. For that to be right, an owner would have to believe the contracts stop paying in the near term, or that the cash is not there or will not be shared.

What we think is happening is a client and a float, not a business in run-off. Kideco paid US$133.8m of the US$164.0m revenue in FY2025, so the customer is disclosed as a related party, and the annual report shows the public holding 26.8% of the shares once the two disclosed holders are counted, which is not a float in which an institution can build a position without moving the price [S2, F23, F1, F47]. The operating record in 2026 is the opposite of a business in decline: overburden removal of 28.3 Mbcm in nine months, gross profit up by more than half, and net profit to owners of US$17.4m that beat the company's own full-year plan by the third quarter [S5, S3, F31].

A mining contractor is a services business wearing a mining label. It does not own the concession, does not sell the coal and does not carry the coal price in its revenue line. It is paid a tariff to strip rock, move coal and keep a fleet running, usually on a multi-year schedule agreed with the concession holder, and its profit is the gap between that tariff and the cost of labour, fuel, tyres, maintenance and subcontractors. The economics therefore behave like a long-term facilities contract with very large equipment attached, and the value is set by the contract term, the counterparty and the utilisation of the fleet.

Three things move the value. The first is the contract book: the overburden work runs to the end of 2029 and the hauling contracts to the end of 2032, so the near-term cash flow is contracted rather than forecast, and the contracted stream is what the life DCF values [S2, p.47]. The second is the balance sheet, which is in net cash and generates more each year than it distributes, so the cash compounds inside the valuation rather than leaking to a terminal value we cannot see [S3, S0]. The third is the dividend, which is discretionary rather than policy-bound and has ranged from a sixth of profit to two thirds, so the yield is an output of the payout decision rather than a promise [S2].

The risk that matters is not the coal price. It is the contract date and the client behind it: a change of control at Kideco, a cut to its production quota, or a re-tender at the 2029 expiry would remove the revenue line rather than compress it [S8, S6, S2, p.47]. Unlike the earlier draft, that case is now in the distribution as a distinct bear at a probability of 20.0% and a value of Rp1,455, and section five shows what happens to the target if that probability doubles.

Samindo Resources is an investment holding company that provides coal-mining services through its subsidiaries. The work is the unglamorous part of the coal chain: overburden removal, which is stripping the rock above the seam; coal getting, which is digging and loading the coal; and coal hauling, which is moving it to the stockpile or the port. The group also sells drilling and geological mapping, rents light vehicles, and holds property [S5]. Revenue is a dollar tariff per cubic metre or per tonne, not a share of the coal price, which is the classification point that shapes every number in this report [S2, S3].

The segment mix moved in 2026 and the move explains the margin. In the nine months to September, group revenue of US$133.1m was led by the overburden removal and coal getting segment, which grew fastest of the three service lines, while the hauling segment earned US$32.9m and vehicle rental fell away as the fleet was moved into the mining operations [S5, S4, F45]. That is why group revenue rose by less than volume: the contractor sold more of the work it does best and less of the work it used to rent out [S5].

One customer is the business. Kideco Jaya Agung paid US$133.8m of the US$164.0m consolidated revenue in FY2025 and US$141.3m the year before, and the filings disclose the balance as a related party because the controlling shareholder of Samindo is also a shareholder in the Kideco group [S2, F23, F24]. The relationship is long-standing rather than new: the overburden and coal-getting contract with Kideco was signed on 30 December 2024 and runs from 31 March 2025 to 31 December 2029, and the company has carried out those services for the same client since 2009; the hauling contracts held by Samindo Utama Kaltim and Trasindo Murni Perkasa run from 31 December 2023 to 31 December 2032 [S2, p.47]. The dates matter more than the volumes: the overburden line, which is the higher-rate work, has a shorter life than the hauling line, and the model now stops the contracted-book DCF exactly where the overburden contract stops.

The asset base is a fleet, not a mine. Fixed assets are trucks, excavators, support equipment and workshops, depreciated at US$14.6m in FY2025, and a meaningful part of the fleet is leased through consumer financing and lease liabilities rather than owned outright [S2, S3]. Capital spending is lumpy because it follows the equipment cycle: US$2.3m of fixed-asset purchases in FY2025, then US$12.0m in the first nine months of 2026 as heavy dump trucks were added for the new contract volume [S2, S3, F36].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. ST International Corporation holds 59.0% of the shares, Low Tuck Kwong holds 14.2% directly, and the public holds 26.8%, which adds exactly to the two disclosed holders and is the float we use [S2, F37, F38, F47]. The operating structure is a set of service companies under the listed holding: overburden and coal getting in PT SIMS Jaya Kaltim, hauling in PT Trasindo Murni Perkasa and PT Samindo Utama Kaltim, drilling in PT Mintec Abadi, vehicle rental in PT Transkon Jaya, and the newer property activity in PT Sentra Terra Indonesia [S5].

Coal-mining services in Indonesia sit between the concession holders, who own the reserve and sell the coal, and the equipment dealers, who finance the fleets. Contracts are usually awarded at a rate per bank cubic metre of overburden or per tonne hauled, with adjustments for haul distance, fuel and volume, and they are renewed on the client's timetable rather than the contractor's. A contractor's bargaining power rises with fleet availability and a safety record, and falls with every year the equipment ages without a renewal.

The client's industry sets the volume, and the volume sets everything else. National coal production is projected at 720 Mt for 2026 against an approved work plan of 600 Mt, which means the government expects the miners to produce more than they were formally permitted, and the domestic market obligation of 25.0% of production sits on top as a claim on tonnage that cannot be exported [S6, F39, F40, F41]. For a contractor the work plan is the demand signal: when the client's quota rises, overburden work rises with it, because the strip ratio does not fall just because the quota does.

The price response has been sharp, and it is the reason the client is busy. After the work-plan cut, the benchmark price for the reference coal grade recovered to US$154/t, and Indonesia's share of traded seaborne coal is 43.0%, which is why a domestic quota decision moves an international price [S7, F42, F43].

The deck's coal view reaches this name through a channel we now quantify rather than assert. The house deck carries Newcastle at US$137.0 a tonne for 2026 and US$105.0 in the long run, which is a fade of roughly a quarter [S0, d.coal.newc]. We do not put that path through the tariff, because the contract is a dollar service fee and contains no coal-price clause; what the fade does is thin the client's margin, and a thinner client approves less stripping and reprices the work at renewal [S2, p.47]. That is precisely the mapping in our bear case: overburden volume halved from FY2027E, the blended rate a quarter lower, and the gross margin back through the FY2025 level, which is what a contractor's book looks like when the client's economics deteriorate through a re-tender. The mapping is worth Rp1,455 a share and is carried at a probability of 20.0% [S2, d.coal.newc].

The contractor market is oligopolistic and equipment-heavy. The large listed contractors work for the big concession groups, the barrier to entry is the capital cost of a fleet plus a safety and environmental record, and the competition is on availability and cost per cubic metre rather than on headline price alone [S2, S5]. Samindo's niche is narrower than the sector: it is effectively a dedicated contractor to one concession, which gives it scheduling certainty and low mobilisation costs, and gives it a concentration that no diversified contractor carries [S2, S8].

The Indonesian coal chain is unusually vertically integrated by international standards. Concession holders often own or affiliate with the contractors and with the barging and port assets that move the coal, and the listed contractor universe is small, so the investable way to own mining services is through a handful of names, most of them tied to a single group. That structure makes contract renewal the dominant risk in the sector, ahead of the coal price itself.

The regulatory channel that matters is the quota, not the royalty. A contractor pays no royalty on the coal because it does not sell the coal; what it faces is the client's work plan, the domestic obligation that diverts tonnage to domestic power stations, and the environmental and reclamation obligations that come with operating a pit [S6, S2]. The domestic obligation is the channel through which a policy decision becomes a volume decision: more tonnage committed at capped domestic prices reduces the client's export revenue and therefore its appetite for stripping [S6].

Competitive position, in five-forces terms. The threat of new entry is low, because a fleet costs capital and the client qualifies contractors on safety and reliability, but the bargaining power of the buyer is very high, because one buyer is almost the whole revenue line and the contract is finite [S2, F23, F1]. The threat of substitutes is low for overburden removal, which cannot be done remotely, and high for the separable services such as vehicle rental and drilling, which the client can insource or buy elsewhere, and which is exactly where the 2026 revenue mix moved away from [S5]. Supplier power sits with the equipment dealers and the labour market rather than with the coal market, since fuel is back-charged to the client and is largely a pass-through [S2].

The moat is a relationship and a fleet, not a resource. A contractor's returns come from fleet utilisation and cost control, and 2026 is a demonstration of both: shorter hauling distances in the pit, better truck availability and lower subcontractor use lifted gross profit from US$25.9m for the whole of FY2025 to US$34.5m in nine months of 2026 [S5, S3, F3, F28]. That is a real but transferable advantage: it renews with the contract, and it disappears if the contract does.

Revenue fell in FY2025 and the reason was operational, not pricing. Overburden removal of 34.0 Mbcm in FY2024 became 31.5 Mbcm in FY2025, coal getting fell from 5.9 Mt to 5.4 Mt, and consolidated revenue went from US$179.6m to US$164.0m as the volume shortfall ran through the tariff [S2, S9, F18, F19, F20, F21]. The company said the overburden result came in below its own work plan, which is the cleanest evidence that this is a contractor with an operating lever rather than a price taker [S2].

The 2026 recovery is volume and cost at the same time. Nine-month revenue of US$133.1m carried gross profit of US$34.5m, against US$25.9m of gross profit on the whole of FY2025, and cost of revenue fell in absolute terms while revenue rose because subcontractor use came down, hauling distances shortened and the fleet the company had bought was available instead of hired [S3, F27, F28, F3]. Administrative expenses went the other way, to US$10.6m in nine months against US$9.5m for the whole of the prior year, because the period carries business development spending on the diversification the company describes [S3, S2, F29, F22].

The gross margin is the assumption the red team was right to challenge, and it has been cut. The file now carries 22.4% for FY2026E and 21.0% from FY2027E, against a nine-month run-rate of US$34.5m on US$133.1m and a best prior year of about a fifth of revenue [S3, F28, F27, S2]. The out-year rate is below the 2026 run-rate and above every one of the four years before it, which is the split between the part of the 2026 gain that persists - an owned rather than hired fleet, shorter hauls, fewer subcontractors, all of them operating choices that last as long as the contract [S2, S5] - and the part that does not, namely truck availability, the mix and the weather. The earlier basis claimed the model did not extrapolate the 2026 improvement while the model held a rate above all history; that inconsistency is gone.

The earnings-quality flag that matters most in this name is depreciation, and the data pack gets it wrong by an order of magnitude. The pack's depreciation line is a fraction of the real charge; the annual report's fixed-asset note shows depreciation of US$14.6m charged through cost of revenue and administrative expenses, with depreciation of right-of-use assets disclosed in addition, and that is the figure we carry [S2, S0, F11]. We restate D&A, capex and the dividend from the notes to the statements and we do not calibrate any cash cost off the pack's figure, which is the discipline that keeps the margin forecast honest [S2, F11, F13, F15].

The pack's operating expense line is the one thing we cannot restate, and the calibration gap it leaves is a forecast step, not a historical artefact. The pack carries an opex line that combines administrative expenses with other operating charges the filing presents elsewhere, so the model's historical EBIT sits below gross profit less filing G&A [S2, F3, F22, S0]. But the model's FY2025A EBITDA margin is 17.9%, identical to the pack's own actual, so the gap the engine reports is the step from that year to the FY2026E forecast margin of 22.3% [S0, S3]. The step is the gross margin, from 15.8% to 22.4%, and it is sourced to the nine months, which delivered US$34.5m of gross profit on US$133.1m of revenue [S3, F28, F27]. Two lines take part of it back: the opex ratio rises from the pack's US$11.2m on US$164.0m of revenue to our 7.9%, which carries the business-development spend, and the D&A ratio falls from US$14.6m on the same revenue to 7.8%, which reduces the add-back. The opex definition change therefore contributes nothing to the step; it is a headwind inside it, and the net step is the gross-margin gain less those two offsets, with no part of it coming from a change of definition. The multiple leg is struck on the pack's LTM EBITDA rather than on the company-reported EBITDA of US$38.8m; on the reported figure the same peer multiple would give a materially higher value, so the cross-check is the conservative end of its own range [S2, F25, S0].

Working capital now reconciles to its own definition. The pack's operating working capital is held at its observed ratio to revenue, and the filing's trade-only definition is narrower: receivables plus inventories less trade payables was materially below the pack figure at both December 2025 and September 2026, while the pack carries other receivable, other payable and related-party balances in the same line [S3, S2]. We cannot restate each component without a quote for each, so the model holds the pack's definition at its observed ratio of 26.5% rather than importing the trade-only ratio; the effect is that FY2026E now books a working-capital build instead of the release the earlier draft assumed, which is the correction the red team asked for [S3, S2].

The forecast is built from volume and tariff, not from a growth rate. We carry 37.7 Mbcm of overburden for FY2026E, which is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month average, and a blended rate of 4.7 dollars per bcm, which is what the nine-month revenue and volume actually produced once the mix shift is allowed for [S3, S5]. That gives revenue of US$177.9m and, at a gross margin of 22.4% that allows for a wet fourth quarter on the FY2025 seasonal shape, EBITDA of US$39.7m and net profit to owners of US$22.5m [S2, S3]. Beyond 2026 we grow volume modestly into the contract and escalate the tariff with dollar inflation rather than with coal, which is the correct escalator for a dollar service fee [S2]. The explicit forecast stops at FY2029E, the last year of the overburden contract, and no post-contract year is modelled as an explicit year [S2, p.47].

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the story and the least appreciated. The company reported EBITDA of US$38.8m in FY2025 against a profit to owners of US$14.9m, while spending only US$2.3m on fixed assets, so the profit was cash and the fleet was not being replaced at book depreciation [S2, F5, F13, F25]. Capital spending then stepped up to US$12.0m in nine months of 2026 for the new trucks, and the balance sheet still ended September with more cash and deposits than it started the year with [S3, F36]. Our forecast has free cash flow of US$14.4m after that capex and working capital, and the cash balance compounds through the explicit period because the payout is only half of profit [S0].

Capital allocation is the open question, and the previous draft was wrong to dismiss part of it. The dividend is set year by year rather than by policy: a sixth of profit in one recent year, roughly half in the others, and US$8.0m paid in FY2025 on the prior year's profit [S2, F15]. Alongside it the company spent US$13.7m on investment property through a new subsidiary and carried a loan to a related party of US$4.2m at September 2026 [S3, F35, F46]. Both are now in the valuation at cost rather than written down to nothing, because the cash has left the balance sheet and the assets remain; what they are not is a return on the mining business, and section six sets out the governance question they raise [S3].

The method set follows the classification, and the classification is now the company's own. A coal producer is valued on a reserve life, a long-run price and a cost-curve position; a contractor is valued on the cash its contracts produce before they expire. We therefore weight a DCF that takes the contracted book to the end of the overburden contract and assumes nothing after it at 50.0%, a FCFF DCF with a terminal value that pays for a renewal at 35.0%, and a contractor peer EV/EBITDA cross-check at 15.0% [S2, p.47, S0]. The split is an explicit statement that the renewal is about as likely as not: the two legs that pay for continuation carry the difference between the contracted-book value and the target, and the P/E method is dropped because profit is dominated by interest income on net cash [S3, F17].

The peer set is four listed Indonesian contractors and no producer. PTRO, DEWA, ABMM and TEBE trade on a median of 11.5x trailing EBITDA, which is a wide distribution - the small names trade at single-digit multiples on EBITDA that is itself depressed, and one trades above thirty - so the leg carries 15.0% and is labelled a market cross-check rather than fair value [S0]. The producers BSSR and INDY are excluded: a producer multiple is a reserve-and-price multiple, which is exactly the error the classification fix removes [S2, p.40]. The multiple is struck on the pack's LTM EBITDA rather than the company-reported US$38.8m, which is the conservative side of the range and is disclosed in section three [S0, F25].

The cost of capital is a dollar build with a concentration premium. The risk-free rate is 4.8%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2%, the Indonesia country premium 2.5% and the industry unlevered beta 1.00, levered to 1.11 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.14; that gives a cost of equity of 13.7%, a pre-tax cost of debt of 6.8%, and a weighted average cost of capital of 12.7% at a debt weight of 11.9% [S2, S3]. On top of the industry beta we carry a company premium of 1.5% for the two risks the beta cannot see: a single client at US$133.8m of US$164.0m of revenue, and a contract whose expiry date is inside the forecast window [S2, p.47, F23, F1]. The premium is stated so it can be removed; without it the weighted value per share would be about four per cent higher, which is the size of the prudence it adds and no more [S0].

The life DCF values only what is signed, and it now ends where the contract ends. Discounting the free cash flow from FY2026E to FY2029E with no terminal value gives an enterprise value of US$62.5m, which after net cash, minorities and the two bridge assets is Rp1,288 a share [S2, p.47, S0]. That is the floor we would defend without any renewal assumption. The earlier draft ran one year past the contract expiry and put a fifth of the floor in a post-contract year; that year is gone, and Rp1,288 is the value of the signed book alone [S2, p.47].

The FCFF DCF with a terminal value gives Rp2,577, with 71.6% of the value in the terminal period, and the gap of -50.0% between the contracted book and the renewal is the renewal question stated in money [S2]. The terminal period is where the hauling contracts that run to 31 December 2032 are carried, because they sit beyond the explicit window, and it is also where the overburden renewal is paid for [S2, p.47, F45]. We are not neutral on the renewal: the company has operated this concession since 2009, the contract was re-signed on 30 December 2024 for the current term, the hauling contracts already run past it, and the group is buying trucks rather than running the fleet down, which is what an operator does when it expects to keep working [S2, p.47, S3, F36]. But a renewal is a negotiation with a related party, so it is paid for in a minority of the weight.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp3,546 on a contractor median of 11.5x, which is 37.6% above the primary FCFF DCF and outside the house's divergence tolerance, so the gap has to be explained rather than smoothed; against the contracted-book DCF it is more than double, which is the same point in a sharper form [S0]. It is the peer set that explains it: four contractors whose EBITDA is at different points in the cycle, one of them close to break-even, and a median that therefore capitalises a mid-cycle number at a multiple earned on trough numbers. We keep it as a cross-check at 15.0% and do not let it set the target; the two DCFs, which disagree by more, carry the rest because they are built on the company's own cash flow [S0, S2].

Blending the three gives a value per share of Rp2,078 before the twelve-month roll, and the weighted target of Rp2,197 rolls to Rp2,271 in the base case and becomes Rp1,757 after the 20.0% illiquidity discount [S0]. That discount is the largest single haircut in the model: the pre-discount target is Rp2,197 and the post-discount target is Rp1,757, so the reader can see both ends of the grid the house uses. It is not a measured number for this stock: the data pack carries no turnover series for the name, and the house ladder applies its widest band when turnover is unknown [S0]. We did not override it, and we flag it as the assumption most likely to be wrong in our favour. The dividend-yield method is dropped from the weights entirely, which the engine records as a change from the industry card: the payout is discretionary, ranging from a sixth to two thirds of profit in recent years, so a yield target would price the payout habit rather than the business [S2, S0].

What the price implies is the most useful figure here. At Rp900 the shares trade on 7.4x trailing earnings, 1.2x trailing EBITDA and 0.6x book, with a trailing yield of 7.3% and a forecast yield of 10.2% on our numbers [S0]. A reverse DCF on the coal price cannot be run against this model, because the model has no coal price in it, which is the consequence of the classification: the equivalent question is what contract life justifies the price, and at an enterprise value of about one year of EBITDA the answer is that the market is pricing a run-off that the contracted book does not support [S0, S2, p.47].

The sensitivity grid shows where the value breaks and what does not matter. A move in the tariff or in volume moves the life DCF by more than the same proportionate move in the margin, because the contractor's cost base is largely fixed once the fleet is in place and the tariff is the revenue line [S0]. The input that matters most is not in the grid at all: it is the weight between the two DCFs, which is a judgement about renewal and is worth more than a full point of gross margin.

The first risk is the contract date, and it now has a number. The overburden contract expires on 31 December 2029 and the renewal is a negotiation rather than an option [S2, p.47]. The bear case assumes it does not survive: overburden volume is cut in half from FY2027E as the client phases the work to a new supplier, the blended rate falls a quarter as the remaining work is repriced, and the gross margin goes back through the FY2025 level as the owned fleet spreads over half the cubic metres; the payout is left where it is, because a dividend cut is a symptom of that stress and not a value driver of its own [S2, F3]. That case is carried at a probability of 20.0% and is worth Rp1,455 a share, against Rp2,271 in the base case and Rp2,628 in the bull case [S0].

The second risk is the client, and it is not diversifiable. Kideco is the counterparty to almost all of the revenue, and its ownership is in play: a reported bid for the Indika stake in Kideco, at a value above US$1,000.0, would put the concession in new hands [S8, F44]. That report is a media rumour, published on 13 October 2026 and not confirmed by any filing, and it is used here as a risk flag and not as a fact [S8, F44]. A new owner would inherit the contracts, but it would also review them, and a contractor whose revenue is one related-party contract has no second customer to fall back on [S2, S8].

The third risk is the quota, not the price. National production is managed through the work plan and the domestic obligation, and a client whose permitted tonnage is cut does less stripping [S6]. The coal price matters through the same channel rather than directly: at US$105.0 long-run Newcastle the client's margin is thinner than it was in 2026, and that is when contractors find their tariffs renegotiated [S2, d.coal.newc]. The mapping from the deck's Newcastle path to our volume and tariff is set out in section two: it is the bear case, not a separate adjustment, and it is worth Rp1,455 [S2, d.coal.newc].

The fourth risk is the balance sheet being used for something other than mining. The company spent US$13.7m on investment property through a new subsidiary and has US$4.2m lent to a related party at September 2026 [S3, F35, F46]. The loan is to PT Tata Hamparan Eka Persada, described in the filing as an entity under common control, at a fixed rate, due 11 April 2028, and it earned US$0.5m of interest in nine months [S3, F46, F48]. Both assets are now valued at cost in the bridge, so the reader can see them, but neither earns a contractor's return, and a dollar spent on unrelated land is a dollar of value at risk rather than a dollar of value created [S3, F35].

The fifth risk is liquidity, and it is the one that explains the price. The public holds 26.8% of the shares and the pack carries no turnover series, so an institution cannot own this comfortably, which is why the discount is applied explicitly and why the shares can trade below any reasonable valuation for longer than a fund's patience lasts [S2, F47, S0].

The scenarios are no longer the mild shock the earlier draft carried. The bear is a contract-loss case and the bull is a renewal case, and both are stated in section four's weights rather than bolted on. The bear takes the shares to Rp1,455, the base to Rp2,271 and the bull to Rp2,628. The bull is entirely operating: the contract is re-signed at the 2029 expiry, the hauling book runs to 2032, volume is fifteen per cent higher, the tariff a few points higher and the gross margin three points above the base [S2, p.47, F45]. The payout is not a source of value in any scenario. Total return is invariant to the dividend by construction, because a higher payout lowers the value per share by the same amount it adds back in the twelve-month return, and paying out net cash removes it from the bridge; the earlier draft's payout shock was worth a rounding error on the target and is gone from the bull [S3, F32, F33]. A special distribution out of the excess cash is a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF, not a valuation gain: it would change what the market pays for cash it does not currently expect to receive, not what the cash is worth.

The test the red team set is what the rating depends on, so we ran it. If the contract-loss probability doubles, from one in five to two in five, and the base case gives up the difference, the weighted target falls by roughly seven per cent and the total return stays near ninety per cent, still well inside the BUY band, because the bear value is itself above the current share price: the equity is mostly cash, and the cash does not care whether the contract is renewed [S3, F32, F33]. That is the honest reason for the rating. The BUY does not rest on the contract being renewed, and it does not rest on the margin holding; it rests on a balance sheet that is worth more than the market capitalisation and a contracted book that is worth more than the price even with no renewal at all [S2, p.47, S3].

For a contractor the operating leverage runs through fleet utilisation rather than through price. A fleet that is fully deployed spreads a fixed cost over more cubic metres, and a fleet that is half idle does the opposite, which is why contractors cut rates to keep utilisation up and why a volume shock is more damaging than a tariff shock of the same size. The asymmetry in our scenarios - a halving of volume against a modest uplift in the bull - is that mechanism stated in the model, not a preference for pessimism.

What changes our view, in order of importance: a renewal of the overburden contract on similar terms would move value from the renewal weight into the contracted one; a loss of the contract would collapse the target toward the cash and the bridge assets, which is the floor the bear case describes; a change of control at Kideco that brought in competing contractors would do the same more slowly; and a decision to distribute the excess cash rather than buy land would not change the DCF value, because the payout is invariant to total return, but it would remove the discount the market applies to cash it does not expect to receive, which is a re-rating rather than a valuation gain [S2, S8, S3]. A rising tariff per cubic metre without a matching rise in the cost base would confirm the 2026 margin as structural rather than cyclical, and we would move the weights accordingly [S3].

Ownership and control are aligned but not dispersed. ST International Corporation holds 59.0% of the shares, Low Tuck Kwong holds 14.2% directly, and the public holds 26.8%, which is the figure the annual report discloses and which we use in place of the data feed's float estimate [S2, F37, F38, F47]. The controlling shareholder is also connected to the client, which is why the Kideco revenue is disclosed as a related-party transaction rather than as an ordinary customer, and why the largest single line of the income statement depends on a relationship rather than a market [S2].

Related-party dealings are the governance issue that needs watching, and the earlier draft described them incorrectly. The Q3 filing shows a loan facility to PT Tata Hamparan Eka Persada, an entity under common control, of which US$4.2m was outstanding at 30 September 2026 after a partial repayment of principal during the period, at a fixed rate and due 11 April 2028, earning US$0.5m of interest in nine months [S3, F46, F48]. That is a related-party exposure and not the third-party lending the earlier draft described; the third-party loan in the same note was the one repaid [S3]. The company also bought land through a new subsidiary for US$13.7m, and books its largest customer as a related party, so the minority is relying on the controlling family to price these transactions fairly [S3, S2, F35].

The mitigant is disclosure rather than structure: the annual report sets out the related-party balances and the terms, the transactions are reviewed by the audit committee, and the auditor signed an unqualified opinion on the accounts [S2]. The dividend record is the best evidence of a shareholder orientation, and it is uneven. The declared payout was a sixth of profit in one recent year and around half in the others, the FY2025 distribution was paid in June 2026, and the shares yield 7.3% on the trailing payment [S2, S0]. A company that pays out half its profit while sitting on net cash is not hoarding, but a company that also buys investment property and lends to a related party is not a pure cash-return story either [S3].

Listed companies with a controlling family shareholder are judged by minority investors on three things: whether related-party transactions are priced at arm's length, whether the dividend policy is a commitment or a mood, and whether the free float is large enough for the stock to be priced by more than one buyer. Samindo scores acceptably on the first two by disclosure and poorly on the third by construction, and the related-party loan sits precisely on the first test.

ESG exposure here is operational rather than financial. The company reports a zero-fatality record for the period, which is the metric that matters most in a business that moves rock with heavy equipment, and its environmental exposure is the reclamation and rehabilitation obligation on the pits it works, which sits with the concession holder rather than with the contractor [S5, S2]. The governance exposure is the one to watch: a small float, a related-party customer and a controlling family with property and lending interests is a combination that discounts the multiple no matter how good the operating year is [S2, S3].

The near-term catalyst is the fourth-quarter operating result and the following year's work plan. The company beat its own plan through September, has added contract volume and put new heavy dump trucks into service for the fourth quarter, so the full-year volumes should confirm the 2026 step-up rather than fade [S5, S4, F36]. The client's work plan is published early in the year and is the demand signal for the period after it [S6].

The second catalyst is the FY2026 dividend. Profit to owners was US$17.4m in nine months, the payout has been around half of profit in the recent normal years, and the payment has been made in June, so the annual meeting is the event at which the cash return is confirmed or not [S3, S2, F30]. A special distribution out of the excess cash would not add to the DCF value, because the payout is invariant to total return by construction, but it is the clearest re-rating catalyst in the file: it would show the market that the cash is reachable, which is the discount the shares carry today [S3, F32, F33].

The third is the Kideco ownership question. A completed sale of the stake would settle who the counterparty is for the rest of the contract, and any review of contractor arrangements that followed would be the largest single swing factor in the equity [S8, S2]. It is a rumour at this stage and we treat it as one [S8, F44].

The fourth is the contract renewal itself. Talks on the overburden contract that runs to the end of 2029 are the value event the life DCF does not pay for, and the first public signal of terms would move the shares more than any quarterly result [S2, p.47]. The precedent is encouraging: the current term was signed on 30 December 2024, ahead of its 31 March 2025 start, with the incumbent on site since 2009 [S2, p.47].

Between updates we monitor overburden volume and coal getting at the client, the blended tariff per cubic metre, the gross margin, capital spending against the fleet plan, the cash and deposit balance, the related-party loan balance, and the payout decision [S3, S2]. The two readings that would change our mind are a falling tariff per cubic metre without a fall in the cost base, which would mean the 2026 margin was cyclical, and a rising share of revenue from anything other than the mining contracts, which would mean the cash is being redeployed away from the business we are valuing [S3, S5, F46].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: The contract does not survive its renewal, and group revenue resets to a fraction of the contracted book. Kideco is re-tendered at the 2029 expiry, or a change of control at the concession brings in a competing contractor, and the overburden volume that SIMS has held since 2009 is cut in half from FY2027E as the client phases the work to a new supplier; the blended tariff falls a quarter as the remaining work is repriced and the mix strips out the higher-rate overburden line; the gross margin drops to the FY2025 level and below as fixed fleet cost spreads over half the cubic metres. The single blended volume input cuts the hauling line with the overburden line, so this is a group-wide shock and not a reset to a surviving hauling book, so it is the harsher reading of the same loss. The payout is left at the base level in every scenario, because a dividend cut is a symptom of the stress and not a value driver of its own. The FCFF terminal value carries the halved business, and the equity is left worth little more than the net cash and the two financial assets in the bridge. This is the state the earlier file gave no probability to.

bull.narrative: The book is renewed and the fleet is kept busy. The overburden contract is re-signed at the 2029 expiry on similar terms, as it was in December 2024, and the client lifts the work plan again after the national quota cut proves orderly; the new heavy dump trucks keep availability high and the hauling contracts run to 2032 with the higher tariff that follows the renewal. The gross margin holds the 2026 gain on the owned fleet and the shorter hauls [S2, S5, F45]. The bull is entirely operating - volume, tariff and margin - because the payout is not a source of value, because total return is invariant to the dividend by construction, so a special distribution out of the US$101.7m of cash and deposits would be a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF, not a leg of it [S3, F32, F33].

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Overburden removed
assumptions.basis: FY2026E of 37.7 Mbcm is built from the nine-month actual, not assumed: 28.32 Mbcm to September 2026, up 23% on 23.04 in the same period of 2025, plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month average of about 9.4 because the company has added 1 Mbcm of overburden work and 1 Mt of coal from its main client and has put new heavy dump trucks into service [S5, S4, F31]. That is 20% above FY2025's 31.49 Mbcm, the year in which overburden came in 11% below the work plan [S2, F18]. FY2027E and FY2028E add 2% a year as the new fleet reaches steady state, then volume is held flat to FY2029E. The series stops in FY2029E because that is the last year of the overburden contract, which expires on 31 December 2029 [S2, p.47]; FY2030E and beyond are not modelled as explicit years, and whatever the hauling contracts deliver in 2030-2032 is carried in the FCFF terminal value rather than in the contracted-book DCF [S2, F45]. The four-year horizon ends with the visible book rather than with a terminal growth assumption.

assumptions.label: Blended revenue per bcm
assumptions.basis: The realised blended rate is revenue divided by overburden removed: US$133.05m of revenue on 28.32 Mbcm to September 2026 is US$4.70 per bcm, against US$5.21 for FY2025 (US$163.97m on 31.49 Mbcm) [S3, F27, S2, F1]. The fall is mix, not tariff: the overburden and coal-getting segment earned US$79.98m on volume up 23%, so its own rate held, while vehicle rental fell away as the fleet was sold into the operations and coal hauling grew more slowly [S5, S4]. We hold the blended rate at US$4.72 for FY2026E, which with the volume above reproduces the run-rate revenue, and then escalate 2% a year with long-run dollar inflation rather than with the coal price, because the contract is a dollar tariff and the deck's Newcastle path is the client's revenue line, not the contractor's [d.coal.newc, d.macro.inflation_usd_lt].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 - share of COGS exposed to Brent
assumptions.basis: Fifteen per cent of cost of revenue is treated as Brent-exposed. The filing shows fuel as a direct operating cost inside cost of revenue, and the group also rents heavy equipment whose rates follow fuel; the rest of the cost base is labour, subcontractors, tyres, maintenance and spare parts, which are rupiah-priced and not oil-linked [S2, F9]. The share is a judgement, disclosed as such, and it is small because most of the 2026 cost reduction came from subcontractor use and hauling distance rather than from fuel [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 - pass-through to tariffs
assumptions.basis: Full pass-through, because the contract is back-charged: the filing carries "receivables from back charge of fuel cost", so fuel consumed for the client is recovered from the client rather than absorbed by the contractor [S2]. With the share at 15% and pass-through at 1.0, a move in Brent lifts cost and tariff together and leaves the margin broadly neutral, which is the correct treatment for a cost-plus fuel arrangement. This differs from the DEWA and PTRO files, where pass-through is partial because those contracts index fuel with a lag [S0].

assumptions.label: Gross margin
assumptions.basis: Twenty-two point four per cent for FY2026E: the nine months delivered 25.9% (gross profit US$34.45m on revenue US$133.05m), but the fourth quarter is the wet season and the FY2025 fourth quarter ran at 10.3% (gross profit US$4.32m on revenue US$41.78m), which is the seasonal shape to carry rather than the nine-month peak [S3, F28, S2, F3]. From FY2027E we step down to 21.0% and hold it: that is below the nine-month 2026 run-rate and above the best of the four prior years (19.0%, 19.1%, 20.1%, 15.8%), and it splits the 2026 gain into the part that persists - shorter hauling distances, lower subcontractor use and an owned rather than hired fleet, which are operating choices that last as long as the contract [S2, S5] - and the part that does not, namely truck availability and the mix, which the client's work plan and the weather drive. The earlier claim that the forecast did not extrapolate the 2026 improvement is withdrawn; 21.0% is still above every historical year, and the bear case takes it back to the FY2025 level.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: General and administrative expenses were 7.9% of revenue in the nine months to September 2026 (US$10.58m of US$133.05m) but only 5.8% in FY2025 (US$9.54m of US$163.97m), because the 2026 period carries US$2.58m of business development spend against US$0.10m a year earlier [S3, F29, F22]. We hold 7.9% for FY2026E and step to 7.5% from FY2027E: the business-development line is project work for the diversification the company describes (new permits and feasibility studies), which we neither extrapolate at the 2026 rate nor assume disappears [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation of fixed assets was US$14.60m in FY2025, 8.9% of revenue, and the nine months of 2026 ran US$10.40m (US$9.92m in cost of revenue plus US$0.48m in G&A), 7.8% of revenue, as older units were sold and replaced [S2, F11, S3]. We use 7.8% for FY2026E, step to 8.0% as the US$11.98m of nine-month capital spending enters service, and settle at 7.8% [S3, F36]. This line is fixed-asset depreciation only: depreciation of right-of-use assets (US$3.63m in FY2025) stays inside cost of revenue and G&A, which is consistent with the cash-flow treatment, where lease repayments sit in financing and are not deducted from free cash flow [S2].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine months of 2026 already carry US$11.98m of fixed-asset purchases, 9.0% of nine-month revenue, against US$2.34m for the whole of FY2025, because the company bought heavy dump trucks to serve the added contract volume [S3, F36, S2, F13]. FY2026E is therefore 9.0%. We then step down to 6.5% and 5.5%: this is a contractor that leases much of its fleet (consumer financing payables of US$9.5m and lease liabilities at September 2026), so sustaining capex is well below the replacement cost of the full fleet, and the FY2022-FY2025 average was 1.9% of revenue [S3, S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The pack's operating working capital was US$43.5m at FY2025A, 26.5% of revenue, and that is the ratio we hold. The filing's trade-only definition is narrower - receivables plus inventories less trade payables of US$35.6m at December 2025 and US$42.4m at September 2026 - and the difference is the other receivable, other payable and related-party balances that the pack carries in the same line [S3, S2]. We cannot restate the pack line without a quote for each component, so we use the pack's own definition at its own observed ratio; at 26.5% of the FY2026E revenue base the model books a working-capital build, not a release, which is the correction the earlier 24.0% assumed. The September receivable of US$33.9m is concentrated on the single main client [S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Twenty-two per cent, the statutory rate: FY2025 carried tax of US$3.57m on pre-tax profit of US$18.56m (19.2%) and the nine months of 2026 carried US$6.22m on US$23.69m (26.3%), the latter lifted by non-deductible foreign-exchange losses [S3, F7, S2]. The two offset, and the company's free float keeps the full rate [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The dollar risk-free rate plus the corporate spread the engine uses in the weighted average cost of capital (4.83% plus 2.00%), 6.83% [d.macro.rf_usd, d.macro.debt_spread_corp]. The observed charge is consistent: finance cost of US$1.72m on interest-bearing debt of US$18.4m at the start of FY2025 is 9.4%, but most of that debt is consumer financing and lease liabilities priced off rupiah rates, not a dollar bond [S2, F16]. The line is immaterial at a debt weight near 12%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of US$4.62m in FY2025 on cash and time deposits of US$98.54m is 4.7%, and the nine months of 2026 ran US$3.03m on US$101.68m, 4.0% annualised, as deposits were rolled at lower dollar rates [S2, F17, S3]. We hold 4.5% on opening cash.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing is assumed. The company is in net cash, repaid short-term borrowings in FY2025 and drew a small bank line of US$3.0m in 2026 that sits against US$101.7m of cash and deposits [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at zero. FY2025 had a net other expense of US$0.7m and the nine months of 2026 carried a US$3.55m foreign-exchange loss against US$1.38m of other income; the loss is a translation and remeasurement item on rupiah balances in a dollar-functional company, not a forecastable operating flow, and carrying the 2026 loss but not a future gain would bias the forecast [S3, S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took US$0.05m of FY2025's US$14.99m profit (0.35%) and hold US$4.19m of the group's US$187.0m equity at September 2026, mostly in Transkon Jaya [S2, S3]. Held at 0.35%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Fifty per cent of net profit: the declared ratios are 49% for FY2024, 16% for FY2023, 50% for FY2022 and 67% for FY2020, so the payout is set year by year rather than by a fixed policy, and the two most recent normal years are 49% and 50% [S2]. The FY2025 profit was paid out at US$8.01m, 54% of US$14.94m, on 11 June 2026 [S2, S3, F15]. We use 50%, not the 54% just paid and not the 16% trough. The payout is held at 50% in the base and in every scenario: total return is invariant to the dividend by construction, because a higher payout lowers the value per share by the amount it adds back in the twelve-month return, and paying out net cash removes it from the bridge, so a distribution is a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF rather than a source of value [S2, S3, F32, F33].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company has not bought back stock and the share count has been 2,206,312,500 for the whole period covered by the filings [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Two per cent, the deck's long-run dollar inflation, applied only in the FCFF cross-check: a dollar-tariff contractor's terminal growth is the tariff escalator, not Indonesian GDP [d.macro.inflation_usd_lt]. The terminal value is also where the hauling contracts that run to 31 December 2032 are carried, because they sit beyond the four-year explicit window [S2, F45]. The life DCF, which carries the larger weight, has no terminal value at all because the overburden contract ends in 2029 [S2, p.47].

challenges.challenge: The company is filed under COAL but MYOH's own annual report (S2 p.40) states the sub-industry as 'Jasa & Perlengkapan Minyak, Gas & Batubara / Oil, Gas & Coal Equipment & Services', which operating configuration maps to MINING_CONTRACTORS whose card is dcf_fcff-primary with a contractor peer set and a 1.0 beta. Tagged COAL, the engine took the producer risk factor and a 0.80 unlevered beta off 19 coal regressions, and the 20%-weighted EV/EBITDA leg used a 6.045x peer median that is BSSR's multiple, a producer, applied to a single-customer contractor. The analyst's own params_basis argues the contractor case; the label should follow it. The direction of the error is to overstate value, on the one call where that matters.
challenges.answer: The classification is corrected and the FATAL is conceded: the company is filed as MINING_CONTRACTORS on its own report sub-industry (S2 p.40), with the contractor card, the contractor peer set and no producer in it. The producer multiple and the 0.80 producer beta are gone. The card change also needs a config classification.forward row, which is the Sector Lead gate and not ours to edit.

challenges.challenge: The scenario set gives zero probability to the event the report itself calls the largest swing factor: loss or non-renewal of the Kideco overburden contract that is 81.6% of revenue. Section 5 says the loss 'is the tail the life DCF already carries', but the life DCF is a method weight, not a probability, and the bear case is a mild single-year shock (volume -10%, tariff -6%, margin -4pp) worth Rp1,821, above the Rp1,792 target. The probability-weighted value of 2,240 therefore contains no state in which the company is worth net cash (~Rp663/share).
challenges.answer: The bear is now a contract-loss case and carries a probability: overburden volume halved from FY2027E, the blended rate a quarter lower, the gross margin back through the FY2025 level and the payout cut, worth far below the old mild-shock bear. We also ran the doubled-probability test the brief requires and state the result in section five: the target falls by about a tenth and the return stays inside the BUY band, because the bear value is itself above the share price.

challenges.challenge: The bridge credits 100% of net cash but omits two owned financial assets that are on the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet: investment property of US$13.70m at cost (S3, F35) and a loan to related party PT Tata Hamparan Eka Persada of US$4.195m (S3 note 10). Together US$17.9m is Rp146/share. The report dismisses the property as 'a governance question and not a valuation asset', but the cash has left the balance sheet and the land remains an asset; the method card requires everything owned to be valued at least at sourced cost.
challenges.answer: Both assets are in valuation.bridge at sourced cost: the investment property at the cash paid (F35) and the related-party loan at its outstanding principal (F46), each at probability 1.0. The property is no longer dismissed in prose and the target impact runs through every method.

challenges.challenge: The report describes the group as having 'lent to third parties at interest' and having 'repaid a third-party loan received'. The Q3 filing shows the reverse pair: a Rp150bn (US$9.7m) facility lent TO related party PT Tata Hamparan Eka Persada at 8.75%, due 11 Apr 2028, with US$4.195m still outstanding at 30 Sep 2026, and a US$9.23m loan to third party PT Duta Perkasa Investindo that was repaid. The related-party loan is exactly the channel section 6 says it is watching, and it is mislabelled as third-party.
challenges.answer: The mislabel is corrected everywhere. THEP is named as an entity under common control, with the facility terms, the partial repayment in the period, the outstanding balance (F46) and the interest income (F48); the third-party loan that was repaid is described as such. Section six now treats it as a related-party exposure, not a generic governance note.

challenges.challenge: The gross-margin assumption is internally contradicted. The basis says 'we do not extrapolate the 2026 improvement to the FY2022 peak of 19.0% of the old cost base or beyond', yet the model holds 22.5% from FY2027E to FY2030E. The last four years' gross margins are 19.0%, 19.1%, 20.1% and 15.8%, so 22.5% is 2.4pp above the best year in the set and is the single largest operating assumption in the model. FY2026E at 22.4% is defensible on the 9M26 actual plus the FY2025 Q4 seasonality; FY2027E-FY2030E is not sourced at that level.
challenges.answer: The out-year gross margin is cut from 22.5% to 21.0%, below the nine-month run-rate and above every one of the last four years, and the contradictory sentence that claimed no extrapolation is removed. The basis now splits the 2026 gain into the part that persists (owned fleet, shorter hauls, fewer subcontractors) and the part that does not.

challenges.challenge: The hauling contracts (SUK and TMP) run to 31 Dec 2032 and produced US$32.86m of 9M26 revenue, 25% of the group, but the model values a single blended rate per overburden bcm only to FY2030 and then stops. Two contracted years of hauling revenue are therefore unvalued, while the report claims the life DCF 'takes the contracted book at its word'. The SIMS overburden contract was itself re-signed on 30 Dec 2024 for 31 Mar 2025-31 Dec 2029 after SIMS worked the concession since 2009 - a renewal track record the 30% renewal weight does not reflect.
challenges.answer: The hauling book is quantified and located rather than asserted: F45 records the nine-month hauling revenue, the assumptions state that hauling sits inside the blended rate through FY2029E and that the 2030-2032 contracted years are carried in the FCFF terminal value, and section four says so. A full segment build is not expressible in the corporate template, which supports one volume and one price series; the explicit statement the challenge allowed as the alternative is what we did.

challenges.challenge: The 'no terminal value' life DCF is not the contracted book: its horizon runs to FY2030E, a full year after the overburden contract expires on 31 Dec 2029, and FY2030 carries volume of 39.2 Mbcm at the flat tariff. The FY2030 PV of US$19.0m is 20.7% of the US$92.0m life-DCF PV, so a fifth of the 'floor' sits outside the contract it claims to take at its word.
challenges.answer: The horizon is four years and the life DCF now ends exactly at the contract expiry, FY2029E; the post-contract FY2030 cash flow that carried a fifth of the old floor is gone. The life DCF values the signed book alone, and section four says so.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 6.045x to FY2025A EBITDA of US$29.37m. The analyst's own fact F25 records company-reported EBITDA of US$38.83m, and the model's FY2025 EBIT of US$14.76m uses the pack opex line of US$11.18m that the report says it cannot restate, against filing G&A of US$9.54m. The multiple leg is therefore struck on a metric 24% below the company's reported figure, and on a producer's multiple; the two errors partly offset but neither is disclosed or tested.
challenges.answer: The multiple is now struck on the contractor peer set with no producer in it, and the mismatch between the pack LTM EBITDA and the company-reported EBITDA is disclosed with the reported figure (F25) and its direction. The engine strikes the multiple on the pack LTM metric and that metric cannot be restated through facts, so the range is shown in prose rather than as a second engine leg; the cross-check is the conservative end of its own range.

challenges.challenge: The NWC input does not reconcile to its stated basis. The basis cites Dec-25 NWC of US$35.6m (21.7% of revenue) and Sep-26 of US$42.4m (24.0%); the model's FY2025A NWC is US$43.5m, 26.5% of revenue, and FY2026E assumes 24.0% of a higher revenue base, which books a US$0.81m working-capital RELEASE. On the stated 24% rule the change would be an outflow of about US$3.3m, and FY2026E FCFF would be US$14.6m rather than US$18.8m - a 22% difference on the line that feeds both DCFs.
challenges.answer: The working-capital ratio is set to the pack definition at its observed 26.5%, which reconciles the opening balance, and FY2026E now books a build instead of the release the 24.0% produced. The basis explains which items sit in the pack line and why the trade-only ratio cannot be restated component by component.

challenges.challenge: The model reads no sector-deck variable, which is right for the revenue line, but the deck's coal view is then never quantified anywhere: Newcastle fades from US$137 (2026) to US$105 long run and the house is NEUTRAL on coal, and the report says this reaches MYOH through the client's appetite for stripping and through tariff resets. Section 5 asserts it; no sensitivity shows it. A contractor on a 3-4 year contract is insulated by months, not years.
challenges.answer: The deck path is mapped to the model and cited to the deck: Newcastle fades by roughly a quarter from the 2026 deck value to the long run, and the transmission is the bear case (volume halved, blended rate a quarter lower, margin back through FY2025), with its value and probability stated in sections two and five. The tariff still carries no coal price, which is the contract, not an omission.

challenges.challenge: F44 ('kideco_deal_value', US$1,000m, period 9M2026A) is sourced to a detik article headlined a rumour and is used in section 5 as 'a reported bid for the Indika stake'. A rumour is not a fact and cannot carry a risk assessment; the period label is also wrong for a point-in-time story. Similarly the deck Newcastle numbers (US$137/2026, US$105 long run) are cited to news source S7 rather than to d.coal.newc, and F42's US$154/t spot quote is labelled 9M2026A.
challenges.answer: F44 is relabelled an unconfirmed media rumour with its publication date and the false 9M2026A period is removed; the spot price F42 is date-stamped to its article date; the Newcastle numbers are cited to the deck variable rather than to a news article.

challenges.challenge: The 20% illiquidity discount is applied to the whole of every method including net cash, and it is the largest single haircut in the model: it removes Rp448/share, and the difference between the 19% free float and the 26.8% public float implied by the two disclosed holders (73.2%) is not explained. No sensitivity shows the target at 0%, 10% and 20%, so the reader cannot see that the entire +109% call is roughly halved by a house convention with no cited basis.
challenges.answer: The float is reconciled to the annual report: the two disclosed holders plus the public line add to the whole (F47), and the report uses that figure rather than the feed estimate. The discount is identified as the house ladder applied at its widest band because the pack carries no turnover series, and both ends of the grid, pre- and post-discount, are shown with placeholders. A 0/10/20 grid is a configuration grid we are not allowed to add.

challenges.challenge: The capital-return case is argued in the prose ('a decision to distribute the excess cash ... would close the gap with no operating change') but not built. Net cash of US$87.2m is 39% of the US$110m market cap; the model pays out 50% and compounds the retained cash at a 4.5% cash yield while discounting everything at a 10.75% cost of equity. A higher or special distribution is mechanically worth more than the same cash retained, and it is the company's own decision, not a market assumption.
challenges.answer: The distribution case is now the bull scenario: the payout returns to the 67% of FY2020, the highest of the last five years, and the value is stated. The scenario framework bounds a payout shock at fifteen points, so the modelled payout is the highest the engine allows, and the report says a special dividend out of net cash would be worth more than this leg.

challenges.challenge: The client control change is described but not quantified. Indika's sale of its Kideco stake (the only source is the S8 rumour) would remove the related-party protection that has kept the work with SIMS since 2009, and a new owner would re-tender rather than inherit. Section 5 gives this risk no probability and no value, so the single largest structural risk to the revenue line after contract expiry is unpriced in the distribution and appears only as a narrative caveat.
challenges.answer: The control-change case is no longer a narrative caveat: it is one of the two routes into the contract-loss bear, which carries a probability and a value, and the report states that a new owner re-tendering at lower rates is the same shock path. The rumour is flagged as unconfirmed in both the fact and the prose.

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 stands verbatim in the text. Section 3 still says "the model's FY2025A EBITDA margin is above the pack's actual by roughly four points, entirely on that line, and it is a historical artefact rather than a forecast input". It is neither: 29.37 on 163.97 is 17.91%, identical to the pack actual, and the 4.39pp gate is FY2026E 22.3% against FY2025A 17.9% - a forecast step, not a historical artefact. The sentence therefore explains away the one calibration gap in the file with a false cause, which is a bias_and_tone defect as well as a text one.
challenges.answer: The false cause is gone. Section 3 now states that the model's FY2025A EBITDA margin is identical to the pack's own actual and that the 4.39pp gate is the forecast step from FY2025A to FY2026E, sourced to the nine-month gross margin of 25.9% (34.45 on 133.05) [S3, F28, F27]. The step is decomposed: the gross margin rises from 15.8% to 22.4%, the opex ratio rises from the pack's 11.2 on 164.0 of revenue to our 7.9%, and the D&A ratio falls from 14.6 on the same revenue to 7.8%, each offsetting about a point. The opex definition change is therefore a headwind inside the step and contributes nothing to it, which is now what the text says.

challenges.challenge: QC Q2 stands verbatim. Section 5 calls the bull "a renewal-and-distribution case" and says "the payout returns to the highest level of the last five years"; section 7 says a decision to distribute the excess cash "would close the gap to our target with no operating change at all". The payout cannot be a source of value: total return is invariant to DPS by construction and paying out net cash removes it from the bridge. QC's re-run with the payout shock removed gives Rp1,758 against Rp1,750, so the claim overstates the bull by an order of magnitude and the Rp2,590 bull is entirely volume / price / margin. This is the sentence a client is most likely to buy the stock on.
challenges.answer: Both fixes are made. The bull is re-specified without the payout shock - volume 1.15, price 1.03 and gross margin +3pp only - and is worth Rp2,628, entirely operating. The payout is held at 50% in every scenario, the bear's payout shock is removed for the same reason, and sections 5 and 7 now state that total return is invariant to the dividend by construction and describe a special distribution as a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF. Removing the payout shock raised the target from Rp1,750 to Rp1,758, which is the size of the overclaim.

challenges.challenge: QC Q4 stands verbatim and is published text, not a note: "If the contract-loss probability doubles to {{val.scenarios.bear.prob|pct}}" renders 20.0%, so the sentence says the probability doubles to the value it already is. The doubled case (bear 40 / base 35 / bull 25, about Rp1,620 and near +90%) exists only in the QC record, not in the report.
challenges.answer: The wrong placeholder is removed. The sentence now expresses the doubled case in words - one in five to two in five - and states the result of the re-run: the weighted target falls by roughly seven per cent to about Rp1,627 and the total return stays near ninety per cent (91.0%), still BUY. Re-run with bear 0.40 / base 0.35 / bull 0.25 against the current shocks.

challenges.challenge: QC Q5 stands. Section 4 says the EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp3,546 "is {vs_primary_pct} above the life DCF": the number rendered is 37.6%, which is the divergence from the primary FCFF DCF of Rp2,577; against the life DCF of Rp1,288 it is +175%. The label and the number still belong to different comparators, and the house tolerance the sentence invokes is measured against the primary method.
challenges.answer: The comparator is corrected. Section 4 now says the 37.6% divergence is measured against the primary FCFF DCF of Rp2,577, which is the method the house tolerance is struck on, and adds that against the contracted-book DCF of Rp1,288 the multiple is more than double. The peer-set width explanation - four contractors at different points in the cycle, one near break-even - is kept unchanged.

challenges.challenge: QC Q6 stands. Section 4 says that without the 1.5% concentration premium "the weighted value per share would be about a seventh higher"; the audit re-run with coe_premium at zero gives Rp2,168 against Rp2,078, +4.3%, a twenty-third. The overstatement is in the conservative direction and inflates the apparent prudence of the valuation at the point where the reader is asked to accept a premium a small contractor does not usually carry.
challenges.answer: The sentence now says about four per cent and the assumptions carry the re-run values. With coe_premium at zero the weighted value per share is Rp2,168 against Rp2,078, +4.3%, a twenty-third and not a seventh; both the report and coe_premium_note quote the same figure.

missing_bull_case.note: The hauling contracts run to 31 Dec 2032 (SUK and TMP, sourced in S2 p.47) and carried US$32.9m of 9M26 revenue, but the model stops at FY2030 and the report explicitly gives them no credit. The 30 Dec 2024 re-award of the SIMS overburden contract for 31 Mar 2025-31 Dec 2029, with SIMS on site since 2009, is evidence of renewal that the prose mentions but the weights do not use. Nor is a capital-return case modelled: net cash of US$87m is 39% of market cap and the model keeps paying 50% and compounding the rest at a 4.5% cash yield inside a 10.8% cost of equity.

missing_bear_case.note: The one risk the report calls the largest swing factor, loss or non-renewal of the Kideco overburden contract (81.6% of FY2025 revenue), is deliberately excluded from the scenario distribution ('the tail the life DCF already carries'). The bear case is a mild single-year shock giving Rp1,821, only 18% below base and above the target. No scenario values the equity at net cash (~Rp663/share) or at a 2029 non-renewal. Section 5 lists five risks without a stated likelihood or rupiah impact for any of them. The related-party cash exposure (THEP loan) is also absent.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E EBITDA margin of 22.3% against FY2025A 17.9% is a 4.39pp calibration gap. The 9M26 evidence supports FY2026E, but FY2027E-FY2030E hold a 22.5% gross margin that is 2.4pp above the best of the last four years (19.0%, 19.1%, 20.1%, 15.8%), and the assumptions text says it will not extrapolate to the FY2022 peak of 19.0% - which the 22.5% number then exceeds. The NWC opening balance also contradicts its stated basis (see C9).

evidence_and_citations.note: Eight load-bearing facts traced and correct: F1/F2 revenue, F3/F4 gross profit, F5 np, F11/F12 D&A (14,602,729 = 13,791,445 COGS + 811,284 G&A), F13 capex, F15 dividends, F23/F24 Kideco revenue, F27-F30 9M26, F32-F36 balance sheet. Three citation problems: F44 is a media rumour given a 9M2026A period and used as fact; the deck Newcastle path is cited to a news article; and the free float of 19.0% is not reconcilable to the two disclosed holders (73.2%, implying 26.8% public). The AR's '31.493 Kbcm' label is a filing typo; the value is right on cross-check.

valuation_method_fit.note: The contractor revenue build (volume x realised USD/bcm, no price driver, no royalty) is the right call and is well argued; the industry tag is not. MYOH's own filing states the sub-industry as 'Jasa & Perlengkapan Minyak, Gas & Batubara', which operating configuration maps to MINING_CONTRACTORS, whose card is dcf_fcff primary with a contractor peer set. Tagged COAL, the engine imports a producer peer median (6.045x, which is BSSR alone) and a producer beta of 0.80. The bridge also omits the investment property and the related-party loan, and the 71% terminal-value share of the FCFF leg is not stress-tested.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is measurably more careful than the conclusion: it states the contract date, the related-party nature of the customer, the discretionary payout and the liquidity problem plainly, and it does not use a single heroic input without naming it. Credit also for building a mirrored scenario set and for showing the reverse-DCF question changes with the classification. The rating survives doubling the bear probability (still ~+100%), but not a contract-loss scenario, which is the point of C2.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model reads no deck variable at all (price_driver blank, royalty_licences empty), which is correct for a tariff contractor, but the consequence is stated rather than modelled: the deck's NEUTRAL coal view and Newcastle fading from US$137 (2026) to US$105 long run reach MYOH through the client's stripping appetite and tariff resets, and the report quantifies neither channel. The DMO/quota discussion in section 2 is sourced and correct.

conservatism_audit.note: Four conservatisms that lower the target without a full source: (i) the 13.70m investment property at cost is excluded from the bridge although the method card says to value everything owned; (ii) the 4.20m loan to related party THEP is excluded; (iii) the 20% liquidity discount is applied to net cash and to every method, removing Rp448/share; (iv) terminal capex is cut to 5.5% against a 9.0% current rate (this one is sourced and accepted). Offsetting unjustified optimism: a 22.5% structural gross margin above all four prior years, and a FY2030 cash flow that sits after the overburden contract expires.

calibration.note: Both BLOCK flags are answered with text that the sources actually support (drift.capex_pct by F36 and the 9M26 purchases; extreme_call by F27-F33), and no blocking flag remains. The calibration gate still reports a 4.39pp EBITDA-margin gap for FY2025A, and the weights.changed WARN against the COAL card is explained in weights_note but is itself evidence that the file is on the wrong card. FY2022A and FY2023A D&A remain un-restated at 0.36 and 0.44, so the historical margin series in the model is not comparable across years.

Optimism: the gross margin of 22.4% FY2026E and 21.0% out is above every one of the four prior years, but 4.9pp below the 9M26 run-rate and sourced to it [S3, F28, F27], and volume grows only 2-4% into a contracted work plan. flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -3.5pp from FY2026E to FY2029E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 3.5pp fall is the shape of a fleet purchase, not a margin of error. The nine months of 2026 already carry US$11.98m of fixed-asset purchases, 9.0% of revenue, for the heavy dump trucks put into service to serve the added 1 Mbcm of overburden and 1 Mt of coal work [S3, F36, S4]. The 5.5% terminal rate is sustaining capex for a contractor that leases much of its fleet, with consumer financing payables of US$9.5m and lease liabilities at September 2026, and it sits above the FY2022-FY2025 average of 1.9% of revenue [S3, S2, F13]. Holding 9% for four years would assume the whole fleet is replaced every year.

flags.message: a.gross_margin: bear -0.15 vs bull 0.03 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: A margin gain of 3pp on an already-above-history 21.0% is the most the 2026 cost base can plausibly deliver, while a lost contract leaves the owned fleet and the workshop fixed cost spread over half the volume, which is why the bear takes the margin back through the FY2025 level rather than by the same 3pp [S2, F3, S3].

flags.message: a.price: bear 0.75 vs bull 1.03 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: Tariff asymmetry follows volume: a renewed contract can reprice a little with dollar inflation, while a re-tender is a competitive process and the incumbency premium is what disappears, so the bear price cut is a quarter against a bull uplift of 3% [S2, p.47, d.macro.inflation_usd_lt]. The base case already escalates the tariff at long-run dollar inflation, so a symmetric bull would double-count the escalator.

flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.5 vs bull 1.15 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The asymmetry is the point of the scenario. A renewal cannot deliver more than a modest increase in a contracted volume that is set by the client's work plan, so the bull adds 15%; a non-renewal removes the entire overburden line that SIMS has held since 2009 [S2, p.47], and the engine's shock bound caps the expression of that at a halving. Mirroring the two would assume the contract can be lost and won by the same amount, which is not how a single-client contractor behaves.

flags.message: expected return +106%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is the sum of three sourced facts, not a target pulled forward. (1) The operating turn is already in the filings: nine-month 2026 revenue of US$133.05m, gross profit of US$34.45m and net profit to owners of US$17.36m, with overburden volume up 23% to 28.32 Mbcm [S3, F27, F28, F30, F31]. (2) The balance sheet is most of the equity value: cash plus time deposits of US$101.68m against interest-bearing debt of about US$14.5m at 30 September 2026, versus a market capitalisation of US$110.0m [S3, F32, F33, S0]. (3) The shares trade on 1.2x trailing EBITDA and 7.4x trailing earnings with a 7.3% trailing yield [S0], while the contracted book alone, with no terminal value and after the house illiquidity discount, is worth more than the share price in our life DCF [S2, p.47]. The reverse DCF cannot bracket the price because the model has no commodity price driver, which is the consequence of the classification: today price implies no view on coal, only that the market pays nothing for a profitable contractor holding net cash.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The card weights are FCFF 0.60, EV/EBITDA 0.25 and P/E 0.15 [S0]. We move 25 points from the FCFF-and-multiple combination into a no-terminal-value DCF, because the overburden contract expires inside the forecast window on 31 December 2029 and the single client is 81.6% of revenue [S2, p.47, F23, F1]; a contractor whose contract ends in four years is worth its contracted cash flow first and its renewal second. P/E is dropped because profit is dominated by interest income on net cash [S3, F17], and the multiple leg is cut to 15% because the four-name peer median is wide [S0].
